## Overview

In spatially resolved transcriptomics, the physical positions of cells or spots
are not incidental — they are biological information. Cells that are physically
adjacent share a local microenvironment, exchange secreted molecules, and
respond to the same spatial cues. Defining signaling neighborhoods by proximity
is therefore more principled than random pairing.

NICHESv2's **spatial mode** uses the coordinates in your data to construct a
neighbor graph, then scores ligand–receptor-mediated (LRM) signaling along
every edge of that graph. Two parameter paths are available:

- **kNN** (`k`): each spot is connected to its *k* nearest neighbors by
  Euclidean distance. Simple and dataset-agnostic.
- **Radius** (`rad`): each spot is connected to all spots within a fixed
  physical radius. More interpretable when the coordinate units have a known
  biological meaning (e.g. micrometres in Visium).

This vignette demonstrates the spatial-mode workflow using the
[`stxBrain`](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data) dataset: ~2,700 Visium
spots from the mouse brain anterior section, with strong spatial tissue
organisation that makes signaling patterns immediately interpretable.

---

## Setup

```{r libraries, eval=FALSE}
library(NICHESv2)
library(SeuratData)   # github.com/satijalab/seurat-data
library(SeuratObject)
```

Install and load the `stxBrain` dataset if you have not done so already:

```{r load-data, eval=FALSE}
# Run once to download (~150 MB)
# SeuratData::InstallData("stxBrain")

data("anterior1")
anterior1 <- UpdateSeuratObject(anterior1)

anterior1
#> An object of class Seurat
#> 31053 features across 2696 samples within 1 assay
#> Active assay: Spatial (31053 features, 0 variable features)
#>  1 layer present: counts
#>  1 spatial field of view present: anterior1
```

---

## Step 1 — Ingest from Seurat

```{r extract, eval=FALSE}
inputs.stx <- extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat(
  seurat.obj = anterior1,
  assay      = "Spatial",
  layer      = "counts",
  verbose    = TRUE
)

dim(inputs.stx$count.mtx)
#> [1] 31053  2696       # genes × spots

colnames(inputs.stx$meta.data)
#> [1] "orig.ident"       "nCount_Spatial"   "nFeature_Spatial"
#> [4] "slice"            "region"
```

### Extracting spatial coordinates

Unlike Seurat objects with dimensionality reduction embeddings, Visium objects
store spatial coordinates in the image slot rather than in cell metadata.
`extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat()` does not automatically transfer them, so we
do this manually before calling `create_NICHESObject()`.

For `VisiumV2` objects (Seurat ≥ 5), coordinates live in
`@images[[i]]@boundaries$centroids`:

```{r coords, eval=FALSE}
# Retrieve barcodes and coordinates from the VisiumV2 image slot
barcodes <- anterior1@images$anterior1@boundaries$centroids@cells
coords   <- anterior1@images$anterior1@boundaries$centroids@coords
rownames(coords) <- barcodes

# Safety check: all barcodes present in meta.data
all(barcodes %in% rownames(inputs.stx$meta.data))
#> [1] TRUE

sum(is.na(coords[rownames(inputs.stx$meta.data), "x"]))
#> [1] 0

# Join coordinates into meta.data by barcode name (safe, not positional)
inputs.stx$meta.data$x <- coords[rownames(inputs.stx$meta.data), "x"]
inputs.stx$meta.data$y <- coords[rownames(inputs.stx$meta.data), "y"]

head(inputs.stx$meta.data[, c("x", "y")], 3)
#>                       x    y
#> AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 7475 8501
#> AAACACCAATAACTGC-1 8553 2788
#> AAACAGAGCGACTCCT-1 3164 7950
```

---

## Step 2 — Choosing a neighborhood radius

NICHESv2 provides `Explore_Radius_Neighborhood()` to help you relate a physical
radius value to the expected number of neighbors per spot, **before** you commit
to building the full object. This is useful because the right radius depends on
your tissue's spot density and coordinate units, which vary across platforms and
experiments.

The function samples a subset of spots, counts neighbors at each radius step,
and returns a plot of mean neighbor count vs. radius:

```{r explore-radius-default, eval=FALSE}
coords.df <- data.frame(
  x = inputs.stx$meta.data$x,
  y = inputs.stx$meta.data$y
)

# Full range — get an overview first
Explore_Radius_Neighborhood(coords.df)
```

The full-range plot shows that large radii (>1000) produce hundreds of neighbors
per spot — biologically implausible and computationally expensive. Zoom into the
actionable range by setting `r.max`:

```{r explore-radius-zoom, eval=FALSE}
# Zoom into the actionable range
Explore_Radius_Neighborhood(coords.df, r.max = 800)
```

The staircase shape is a feature of the Visium hexagonal grid: spots are
arranged in concentric hexagonal rings, so neighbor count increases in discrete
jumps rather than smoothly. Reading the zoomed plot:

- **Radius ~200** → ~6 neighbors per spot (equivalent to the first hexagonal ring)
- **Radius ~400** → ~25–30 neighbors (two rings)
- **Radius ~600** → ~50–60 neighbors (three rings)

For a first analysis, **6 immediate neighbors** is a natural starting point —
it captures direct physical contacts without diluting the signal with distal
spots. In this vignette we use `k = 6` (kNN mode) for simplicity and
reproducibility, which is equivalent to radius ~200 for this dataset:

```{r sample-split-note, eval=FALSE}
# Note on sample splitting:
# This dataset contains a single tissue section, so sample.col = NULL.
# If your experiment includes multiple sections or capture areas, always
# set sample.col to avoid edges being constructed across sections.
```

---

## Step 3 — Build the NICHESObject

```{r create-object, eval=FALSE}
niches.stx <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx  = inputs.stx$count.mtx,
  meta.data  = inputs.stx$meta.data,
  LRM.db     = load_LRM_database("fantom5", species = "mouse"),
  mode       = "spatial",
  species    = "mouse",
  sample.col = NULL,
  k          = 6L,
  method     = "product",
  n.cores    = 4L,
  verbose    = TRUE
)
```

`load_LRM_database("fantom5", species = "mouse")` loads the bundled FANTOM5
ligand–receptor database for mouse — no internet connection required.

---

## Step 4 — Inspect the result

```{r print-object, eval=FALSE}
print(niches.stx)
#> -- NICHESObject --------------------------------------------
#>   Cells        : 2696  (2696 non-empty)
#>   Genes        : 31053  (20467 valid)
#>   Edges        : 18500  (18495 non-empty)
#>   LRM pairs    : 2251  (1827 valid)
#>   Segmentation : none
#>
#>   Slot summary:
#>     $cell.list     -- character vector of cell barcodes
#>     $cell.data     -- (cell, gene, score, score.norm) [sparse]
#>     $cell.meta     -- per-cell metadata
#>     $edge.list     -- (edge, SendingCell, ReceivingCell)
#>     $edge.data     -- (edge, LRM, score, score.norm) [sparse]
#>     $edge.meta     -- per-edge metadata with Sending/Receiving/Joint cols
#>     $neighborhood.* -- reserved (NULL)
#>     $gene.list     -- character vector of gene names
#>     $gene.meta     -- per-gene metadata
#>     $LRM.list      -- character vector of 'ligand|receptor' pairs
#>     $LRM.meta      -- per-LRM metadata
#>     $segmentation  -- sf object of cell polygons, or NULL
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
```

In spatial mode, `$edge.data` carries the same `edge | LRM | score | score.norm`
structure as sampled mode, but each edge now corresponds to a physically proximal
spot pair. The sending spot's coordinates are stored in `$edge.meta`:

```{r edge-data, eval=FALSE}
head(niches.stx$edge.data, 3)
#> Key: <edge, LRM>
#>                                          edge          LRM score  score.norm
#>                                        <char>       <char> <num>       <num>
#> 1: AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1|AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 Adam15|Itgav     4 0.003798670
#> 2: AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1|AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1    Apoe|Lrp1   148 0.140550810
#> 3: AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1|AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1   Apoe|Sorl1    37 0.035137700
```

---

## Step 5 — In situ connectivity map

`CellToCell_InSitu_Single_LRM()` maps the LRM score of every edge onto the
tissue coordinate system, drawing each edge as a coloured line segment between
sending and receiving spots.

Here we visualise **Gnas|Adcy1** — Gnas (G protein alpha subunit) signalling
to Adcy1 (adenylate cyclase 1). The resulting map reveals a striking cortical
arc: high-scoring edges concentrate in the cortex, which wraps around subcortical
structures along the lateral and inferior edges of the anterior section. This
spatial pattern is consistent with the known high expression of adenylate
cyclase in cortical neurons and reflects the power of spatial mode to localise
signalling to anatomically coherent regions.

```{r insitu-plot, eval=FALSE}
CellToCell_InSitu_Single_LRM(
  niches.obj    = niches.stx,
  LRM           = "Gnas|Adcy1",
  bg.alpha      = 0.3,
  bg.linewidth  = 0.2,
  sig.linewidth = 0.3,
  sig.alpha     = 0.7
)
```
